'''''Potentilla erecta''''' (syn. '''''Tormentilla erecta''''', '''''Potentilla laeta''''', '''''Potentilla tormentilla''''', known as the ('''common''') '''tormentil''', '''septfoil''',<ref>[http://www.thefreedictionary.com/Septfoil Septfoil - definition of Septfoil by the Free Online Dictionary, Thesaurus and Encyclopedia<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> or '''erect cinquefoil'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=POER81|taxon=Potentilla erecta|accessdate=13 October 2015}}</ref>) is a herbaceous [[perennial plant]] belonging to the rose family ([[Rosaceae]]).

==Description==
''Potentilla erecta'' is a low, clump-forming plant with slender, procumbent to arcuately upright stalks, growing {{convert|10|–|30|cm}} tall and with non-rooting runners. It grows wild predominantly in [[Europe]] and western [[Asia]][http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/rosa/poten/poteerev.jpg], mostly on acid soils and in a wide variety of habitats such as mountains, heaths, meadows, sandy soils, and dunes.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book | last=Stace | first= C. A. | author-link = Stace, C. A.|date= 2010 | title=New Flora of the British Isles, 3rd edition | publisher= Cambridge University Press | location=Cambridge, U.K. | isbn=9780521707725 | page=256 }}</ref>

This plant flowers from May to August or September. There is one yellow, {{convert|7|–|11|mm}} wide flower, growing at the tip of a long stalk. There are almost always four notched [[petal]]s, each between 3 and 6 mm long. Four petals are rather uncommon in the rose family. The petals are somewhat longer than the [[sepal]]s. There are 20–25 [[stamen]]s.

The radical [[Leaf|leaves]] have a long [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]], whilst the leaves on the flowering stalks are usually sessile or with short petioles. The glossy leaves are alternate, ternate, consisting of three obovate leaflets with serrated margins. The paired [[stipule]]s are leaflike and palmately lobed.

There are 2–8 dry, inedible fruits.
[[File:Potentilla erecta (root).jpg|thumb|[[Rhizome]] of ''Potentilla erecta'']]

==Distribution==
===Europe===
''Potentilla erecta'' is found wild throughout Europe, Scandinavia, and West Asia.<ref name=dvf>{{cite web |author=Arne Anderberg |title=Den Virtuella Floran: Blodrot, ''Potentilla erecta'' (L.) Räusch. |date=2005 |url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/rosa/poten/poteere.html |access-date=13 November 2019 }}</ref>

''Potentilla erecta'' is almost ubiquitous in the British Isles, recorded in almost all 10 km squares except close to [[the Wash]].[http://sppaccounts.bsbi.org.uk/content/potentilla-erecta] and is listed as a species of least concern.<ref name=Cheffings>{{cite web|last1=Cheffings|first1=C.|last2=Farrell|first2=L.|year=2005|title=The Vascular plant red data list for Great Britain|page=82|url=http://jncc.defra.gov.uk/page-3354#download/}}</ref> It is very common in grasslands, heaths, moors, mountains, bogs including roadsides and pastures, mostly on acidic soils,<ref name=Stace /> but avoiding chalk.<ref name=Rose>{{cite book|last=Rose|first=F.|year=2006|title=The Wild Flower Key.|location=London|publisher=Penguin|pages=258–259|isbn=978-0723251750}}</ref> It is a component of [[British National Vegetation Classification]] community M25 (''Molinia caerulea''–''Potentilla erecta'' mire).

===North America===
In North America ''Potentilla erecta'' is found in the east as an introduced species.

==Uses==
The rhizomatous [[root]] is thick.{{clarification needed|reason=how thick?|date=July 2020}}  It has little value for food use  because of its bitterness and low caloric value. The roots are a main ingredient of a [[bitters|bitter liqueur]] from [[Bavaria]] and the Black Forest area, called [[Blutwurz]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.food-from-bavaria.de/de/reg_spez/einzelprodukt.php?an=203&display_lang=en|title=Blutwurz|publisher=Bayerisches Staatsministerium für Ernährung, Landwirtschaft und Forsten|access-date=June 4, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726024316/http://www.food-from-bavaria.de/de/reg_spez/einzelprodukt.php?an=203&display_lang=en|archive-date=July 26, 2011}}</ref> It is also used in Ukraine along with honey in [[horilka]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ackland |first1=Tony |title=Ukrainian Alcoholic Beverages |url=https://homedistiller.org/flavor/ukraine |website=Home Distillation of Alcohol |publisher=homedistiller.org |access-date=15 January 2019}}</ref>
The plant is used in herbal medicine as an [[astringent]] because of its [[tannin]] content,{{citation needed|date=October 2011}} which is unusually high for a [[herbaceous]] plant.{{citation needed|date=July 2020}} Structurally-related [[phlobaphene]]s, used as a red dye for leather known as ''tormentil red'', can be extracted from the root of the common tormentil along with the triterpene alcohol [[tormentiol]].<ref name=Lund>{{cite journal |author1=Lund, K. |author2=Rimpler, H. |date=1985 |title=Tormentillwurzel |journal=Deutsche Apotheke Zeitung |volume=125 |issue=3 |pages=105–107}}</ref>  Aqueous extracts of the rhizomes are reported to have low toxicity in rats and mice.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Shushunov S, Balashov L|author2=Kravtsova A |author3=Krasnogorsky I |author4=Latté KP |author5=Vasiliev A |title=Determination of acute toxicity of the aqueous extract of Potentilla erecta (Tormentil) rhizomes in rats and mice|publisher=Journal of Medical Food|date=October 2009|volume=12|issue=5|pages=1173–6|doi=10.1089/jmf.2008.0281 |pmid=19857087 |journal=J Med Food}}</ref> Research into the plant during 2026 indicates that other significant medicinal uses may be indicated.<ref>Kavita Gadar, Maria Pigott, et al, ''[https://www.microbiologyresearch.org/content/journal/micro/10.1099/mic.0.001675 Bogland plant Tormentil inhibits multidrug-resistant pathogen growth and potentiates antibiotics by disrupting iron homeostasis Open Access]'', Microbiology Society, Microbiology, Volume 172, Issue 3, March 23, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1099/mic.0.001675</ref>
